name: AI Workload Readiness
description: Scores the discipline of the pre-engagement conversation that defines how an AI workload redesign will be measured: scoping the unit, capturing the baseline, naming the role change, fixing the success measures, diagnosing adoption, and putting one name against the result.

criteria.name: Workload Scoping
criteria.description: Whether the rep narrows the conversation to a single workload with a trigger, a finished state, and a countable volume.

levels.label: Poor
levels.description: Accepts a department or function as the scope ("customer service", "the claims team") and never narrows it.

levels.label: Below Average
levels.description: Names a process but leaves the trigger and finished state undefined, so two people would describe different work.

levels.label: Adequate
levels.description: Defines one workload with a start and an end, but does not establish how many instances run per month.

levels.label: Good
levels.description: Defines the workload, its trigger, its finished state, and gets a volume figure from the client.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Does all of that and applies the narrowing test out loud — splits the workload when the client's description could produce two different instances, and says plainly that an uncountable workload cannot be measured.

criteria.name: Baseline Capture
criteria.description: Whether the rep gets before-numbers with a stated source and an honest confidence level, rather than estimates offered as fact.

levels.label: Poor
levels.description: Takes no current-state numbers at all, or accepts a vague "it takes about a day" without pressing.

levels.label: Below Average
levels.description: Collects one or two figures but never asks where they came from, so they cannot be re-measured later.

levels.label: Adequate
levels.description: Collects several measures with sources, but does not distinguish a timed sample from a manager's guess.

levels.label: Good
levels.description: Collects time, cost, and quality measures, names the source of each, and scores confidence.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Does all of that and is willing to stop — tells the client that with fewer than three high-confidence measures the workload is not yet measurable, and proposes instrumenting it before committing to targets.

criteria.name: Role Delta
criteria.description: Whether the rep establishes what changes for the people who do the work, including what comes off their plate and what they are judged on.

levels.label: Poor
levels.description: Treats the redesign as a systems change. Never asks who performs the work or what changes for them.

levels.label: Below Average
levels.description: Mentions training or communication as the people component, but does not examine the role itself.

levels.label: Adequate
levels.description: Establishes what each role will do after the change, but not what they stop doing.

levels.label: Good
levels.description: Covers what they do after, what they stop doing, and what is genuinely new to them.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Does all of that and raises the two uncomfortable rows directly — what the person will now be judged on and by whom, and what they could reasonably fear losing — treating both as design problems rather than communication problems.

criteria.name: Success Definition
criteria.description: Whether the rep drives to a small, signed set of measures with baselines, targets, dates, and a fixed measurement method.

levels.label: Poor
levels.description: Leaves success undefined, or settles for directional language like "improved efficiency" and "better outcomes".

levels.label: Below Average
levels.description: Proposes measures but no baselines or dates, so nothing can be compared at the end.

levels.label: Adequate
levels.description: Gets three to five measures with baselines and targets, but all of them are speed or cost measures.

levels.label: Good
levels.description: Includes a quality or risk measure and an adoption measure alongside the efficiency measures, each with a date.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Does all of that, fixes the measurement method to match the baseline method, names who agrees each target, and gets agreement in advance on what happens if a target is missed.

criteria.name: Adoption Diagnosis
criteria.description: Whether the rep treats non-adoption as something to diagnose with evidence rather than something to solve with training.

levels.label: Poor
levels.description: Treats adoption as a communication or change-fatigue issue. Offers a comms plan or a town hall.

levels.label: Below Average
levels.description: Assumes the problem is skills and proposes training before establishing any cause.

levels.label: Adequate
levels.description: Acknowledges adoption risk and proposes to survey or interview people, but without a defined construct.

levels.label: Good
levels.description: Names specific drivers — role clarity, line of sight, perceived threat, self-efficacy — and proposes measuring them before and after.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Does all of that and distinguishes which driver a given symptom points to, explaining that training only moves self-efficacy and that low role clarity sends the work back to the role design.

criteria.name: Measurement Ownership
criteria.description: Whether the rep puts one named person against the after-numbers and accepts accountability rather than leaving measurement with the client.

levels.label: Poor
levels.description: Leaves measurement unassigned, or assigns it to "the team" or a steering committee.

levels.label: Below Average
levels.description: Assigns it to the client by default, with no access, date, or consequence attached.

levels.label: Adequate
levels.description: Names one person and a due date, but does not secure the access they would need to produce the numbers.

levels.label: Good
levels.description: Names one owner, the date, the reporting line, and the access required.

levels.label: Excellent
levels.description: Takes the obligation onto the supplier side and commits in advance that the numbers will be reported whether or not they meet the targets — turning the attribution argument into an accountability the client can hold them to.
